 Your guide to frequently used Election Day terminology
 By Ethan Cohen and Zachary B. Wolf 
 As you watch the results come in tonight, there could be some terms that come up frequently.
 Here’s a guide of election terminology to keep handy:
 Incumbent: A lawmaker or elected official running for reelection. They currently hold the seat they are running for.
 Flipped seat or pickup: A flipped seat is one in the House or Senate that voters take from one party and entrust to the other party. But, because of redistricting or resignations, there are some races that are “open,” meaning there isn’t an incumbent.
 Special election: When a senator retires, dies or leaves office before his or her term ends, the state’s governor usually appoints a placeholder to fill the seat, but there needs to be an election for the full term. South Carolina’s Senate race is a special election, after the death of late Sen. Lindsey Graham. There is also a special election in Ohio to fill the Senate seat that was previously held by Vice President JD Vance, for example.
 Ranked choice voting : A number of cities and states are experimenting with ways to give voters more access to the political process and to potentially depolarize politics. Ranked choice voting is a system in place for most elections in Maine and Alaska where voters rank their choices in order of preference instead of picking a single candidate.

 Top Trump administration officials' views on voting 
 0:17
 The Trump administration has undertaken an unprecedented effort to inject the federal government into state elections as it hunts for voter fraud — and to help President Donald Trump continue his baseless quest to try to prove the 2020 election was rigged and stolen from him.
 Election officials and Democratic lawmakers fear that the Trump administration’s aggressive actions could spill into Election Day and voter intimidation — and that dubious claims of mass voter fraud will be used to cast doubt on the election results if they go poorly for Trump and the GOP.
 CNN has reviewed what five outspoken officials leading the effort — including the president — have said in TV interviews, podcast appearances and speeches about voter fraud and their attempts to find it ahead of the midterms, how their claims about widespread issues of fraud often don’t add up, and what actions they say their agencies or the federal government may take this week or beyond.

 Everyone keeps talking about the “balance of power.” Here’s what that means
 By Ethan Cohen and Zachary B. Wolf 
 Political parties have more power when they control the House or Senate by winning a majority of the seats in that chamber.
 The party in power controls committees that write legislation and decides which measures will get a vote on the floor.
 In the House, the party with at least 218 seats has the majority and, assuming it can unite behind one candidate, selects the Speaker of the House. In the Senate, the party with 51 votes has the majority.
 Why are only a third of senators up for election? 
 Senators serve six-year terms, and there are federal elections every two years. The seats are broken up into three classes, and about a third of the Senate is on the ballot every two years.
 Why are all 435 House members up for election every two years? 
 The House of Representatives is the piece of the federal government that is closest to the people. Putting House members up for election every two years allows voters more direct and immediate control of the direction of their government.

 Talarico says he and his supporters are 'underdogs' in final Texas rally
 Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico and his Republican rival Ken Paxton held their final rallies Monday night, making a last push for voter support.
 1:12
 • Source:
 CNN 
 Talarico says he and his supporters are 'underdogs' in final Texas rally 
 1:12
 Ken Paxton: In final remarks to supporters, he said the Texas Senate midterm is about “safeguarding our way of life,” and cautioned that “both sides have completely different objectives for this country.” Citing his record as attorney general of the state, Paxton said his plan would put money in Texans’ pockets while Talarico’s plan would take money from them.
 Mary Peltola: The Alaskan Democratic Senate candidate’s campaign has been marred by controversy after a report on its alleged involvement in recruiting another man named Dan Sullivan to run for Senate to confuse voters. Peltola has denied knowing anything about the alleged scheme. “We’ve kept this focused on Alaskans. We are not interested in smearing our friends and neighbors, and future colleagues,” she told supporters. 
 Sen. Dan Sullivan: The Republican cast Alaska as “the firewall for freedom” in his closing message, emphasizing the country is focused on the race as it could decide control of the upper chamber.
 Adam Hamilton: The Democratic nominee for Kansas Senate will be writing both a concession and a victory speech , he said, but also enthusiastically pointed to recent polls looking good for his campaign. Hamilton, who is running against Sen. Roger Marshall, is hoping to be the first Kansas Democrat elected to the US Senate since 1932.
 Troy Jackson: The Maine Democratic Senate candidate rallied supporters in Portland, 100 days after securing the Democratic nomination . Jackson became the party’s nominee after Graham Platner exited the race following a string of controversies, including a sexual assault allegation he’s denied. Jackson faces the GOP incumbent Sen. Susan Collins in the closely watched race that could determine control of the Senate.
 Annie Andrews: Hundreds of supporters of the South Carolina Democrat gathered in Charleston to close out what has been an unexpectedly competitive Senate campaign in a state that voted for Trump by nearly 18 points in 2024. Andrews took thinly veiled shots at her opponent, Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to fill the remainder of her late brother’s Senate term in July before being asked by to run for this full six-year Senate term.

 US conducts limited strikes against Iran on election eve, officials say
 By Alayna Treene and Kevin Liptak 
 An aerial view of the Iranian shores and the island of Qeshm in the strait of Hormuz, on December 10, 2023. 
 Nicolas Economou/Reuters 
 The US military carried out limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island on Monday, three US officials told CNN, characterizing the action as defensive in nature and meant to protect American assets in the region.
 It does not appear to be the kind of major combat operation that officials have been contemplating . “This was a defensive measure for Iranians using surface to air missiles against US assets,” one US official said.
 But the new action, on the eve of Election Day, is a reminder that the situation in Iran is still unresolved, and combat is still very much on the table.
 One person familiar with the matter said the administration deliberately kept the attack under wraps in an effort not to overstate the defensive move.
 President Donald Trump on Monday suggested that diplomacy with Tehran is still at work, saying an agreement “could happen.” He did not address the strikes in an appearance on Fox News that aired Monday night, but did say the US “might have to go after” Pickaxe Mountain , Iran’s suspected underground nuclear site.
 Global oil prices are spiking as the war drags on, with gasoline and diesel prices on track to be the most expensive of any US Election Day in history. Those increasingly high prices have been front and center in campaigns throughout the country.
 CNN has spoken with many voters, including at the president’s rallies, who have pointed to the war’s impact on gas prices and the cost of living as a major issue in the election. The issue has prompted some Republicans facing tough elections to distance themselves from the president’s stance on the war.
